Case-based lecture (the course's 453 lecture file): every case is a question slide followed by an explanation slide. The cases are grouped by topic here; the case numbers follow the order of the file. The file gives the explanation without the letter, so the Answer line is taken from the explanation.

1. Recognising the deteriorating patient

Case 1 — Confusion after emergency hemicolectomy

A 72-year-old man is 18 hours after emergency right hemicolectomy for caecal perforation. He becomes confused. HR 118/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, RR 30/min, temperature 38.2°C, oxygen saturation 94% on 4 L/min nasal oxygen. Urine output has fallen to 15 mL/hour. Lactate is 4.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

  • A. Start maintenance IV fluid and repeat observations in 4 hours
  • B. Give paracetamol, as fever is the most likely explanation
  • C. Activate urgent senior review and begin simultaneous ABCDE resuscitation, sepsis assessment, and source evaluation
  • D. Arrange CT abdomen only after the morning surgical round
  • E. Give IV furosemide for oliguria

Answer: C · Activate urgent senior review and begin simultaneous ABCDE resuscitation, sepsis assessment, and source evaluation

This is organ dysfunction with likely shock: altered mentation, tachypnoea, oliguria, and hyperlactataemia. The patient may have sepsis, ongoing intra-abdominal contamination, bleeding, aspiration, or mixed pathology. Begin ABCDE, obtain access and blood tests/cultures, administer oxygen and appropriate antimicrobials, assess fluid responsiveness, involve senior surgery/anaesthesia/ICU, and urgently determine whether source control is required.

  • Respiratory distress after extubation (accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing, confusion) → reintubate immediately. 439

Case 4 — Rising lactate with a normal blood pressure

A 59-year-old man is postoperative day 2 after low anterior resection. He is tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Lactate rises from 2.2 to 4.7 mmol/L despite 2 L balanced crystalloid. BP is now 108/68 mmHg. Which statement is most accurate?

  • A. A normal blood pressure excludes ongoing shock
  • B. Rising lactate may indicate persistent hypoperfusion despite preserved blood pressure
  • C. The lactate must be due to hepatic failure
  • D. Further assessment is unnecessary because the MAP is above 65 mmHg
  • E. Lactate is useful only in trauma patients

Answer: B · Rising lactate may indicate persistent hypoperfusion despite preserved blood pressure

A patient may remain in compensated shock despite an apparently acceptable arterial pressure. Rising lactate should prompt reassessment for ongoing bleeding, abdominal sepsis, bowel ischaemia, inadequate oxygen delivery, cardiac dysfunction, excessive adrenergic stimulation, impaired lactate clearance, or a mixed shock state.

  • MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP): BP 80/50 → 60. 438 ×2 437 Final
  • Oliguria after only 350 cc in a 95 kg woman → inadequate resuscitation. 441
  • Persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin → look for sepsis. 438 ×4 435 Final

Case 33 — MAP on target but still hypoperfused

A patient in septic shock has MAP 70 mmHg on norepinephrine, but remains mottled with oliguria and increasing lactate. Which statement is most appropriate?

  • A. MAP alone proves adequate resuscitation
  • B. The vasopressor should be stopped because MAP is above 65 mmHg
  • C. Reassess macro- and microcirculatory perfusion, cardiac output, fluid responsiveness, source control, and alternative causes of lactataemia
  • D. Give fluids without any further evaluation
  • E. Ignore urine output if the MAP is acceptable

Answer: C · Reassess macro- and microcirculatory perfusion, cardiac output, fluid responsiveness, source control, and alternative causes of lactataemia

Blood pressure is a target, not the sole marker of adequate perfusion. Persistent signs of impaired perfusion require reassessment of cardiac output, preload responsiveness, vasoplegia, ventricular dysfunction, haemorrhage, source control, and tissue-level perfusion. Capillary refill, skin temperature/mottling, lactate trajectory, urine output, and mental state all

  • Most accurate marker of inadequate tissue perfusion → lactate; best monitor of adequate resuscitation → urine output. 438 ×2 434 ×5 431 ×3

Case 37 — Worse again after initial improvement

A patient with abdominal sepsis appears initially to improve after fluid and antibiotics. Four hours later, vasopressor requirements rise and lactate increases. What is the best next cognitive step?

  • A. Assume the original diagnosis and management are correct
  • B. Attribute all deterioration to delayed antibiotic effect
  • C. Reassess the diagnosis, adequacy of resuscitation, and especially adequacy of source control
  • D. Stop monitoring because treatment has already been initiated
  • E. Repeat only the full blood count

Answer: C · Reassess the diagnosis, adequacy of resuscitation, and especially adequacy of source control

Deterioration after an initial response should prompt a deliberate diagnostic reset. Consider persistent contamination, missed ischaemia, occult haemorrhage, resistant infection, cardiogenic component, pulmonary embolism, line complication, or an alternative diagnosis.

Case 39 — Culture-negative septic shock

A patient has presumed sepsis, but blood cultures are negative and the patient remains in shock. Which is the best principle?

  • A. Negative cultures exclude infection and mandate stopping all treatment
  • B. Continue treating the syndrome while reassessing source, antimicrobial adequacy, and alternative non-infectious causes of shock
  • C. Culture-negative sepsis cannot occur
  • D. Start every available antibiotic indefinitely
  • E. Do not seek source control if cultures are negative

Answer: B · Continue treating the syndrome while reassessing source, antimicrobial adequacy, and alternative non-infectious causes of shock

Culture-negative sepsis is common. Microbiology must be integrated with the clinical course, imaging, operative findings, antimicrobial exposure, immune status, and alternative diagnoses. Persistent shock still demands reassessment for a surgically remediable source.

Case 36 — Who needs ICU-level care?

Which finding most strongly suggests that a patient with sepsis requires ICU-level care?

  • A. Fever of 38.1°C with normal perfusion
  • B. A single raised CRP concentration
  • C. Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors after initial resuscitation
  • D. A mildly raised white-cell count
  • E. Need for oral antibiotics

Answer: C · Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors after initial resuscitation

Vasopressor-dependent shock, escalating oxygen/ventilatory requirements, altered consciousness, worsening acidosis/lactate, severe organ dysfunction, or need for invasive monitoring are clear indicators for critical-care involvement.

  • Hourly ICU monitoring essential: MAP. 439 ×2

Case 38 — Why an arterial line?

A surgical registrar asks a student to explain why a patient needs an arterial line. Which answer is best?

  • A. It replaces the need for clinical examination
  • B. It permits beat-to-beat pressure monitoring and repeated blood sampling in unstable shock or vasopressor use
  • C. It is required in every patient with a fever
  • D. It directly measures intravascular volume
  • E. It prevents the need for ICU referral

Answer: B · It permits beat-to-beat pressure monitoring and repeated blood sampling in unstable shock or vasopressor use

An arterial line improves monitoring precision when blood pressure is unstable or vasopressors are required and facilitates repeated blood-gas/lactate sampling. It does not measure preload or replace clinical reassessment and source-control decisions.

  • Signs of shock are determined by the amount of intravascular volume lost. 431
  • ICU patient (ventilated > 48 h, on vasopressors) bleeding from the NG tube → prevent with gastric acid suppression (stress ulcer prophylaxis). 439

Case 40 — The framework in one sentence

A student is asked to summarise the approach to a deteriorating surgical patient. Which answer is best?

  • A. “Order tests first, then intervene when the diagnosis is certain.”
  • B. “Treat hypotension with fluid in every patient.”
  • C. “Use ABCDE; recognise shock and organ dysfunction early; resuscitate while diagnosing; identify the shock phenotype and surgical source; obtain timely haemorrhage control or source control; reassess response continuously; and escalate early.”
  • D. “Focus on the wound and drain because surgical patients usually deteriorate from local complications only.”
  • E. “A normal blood pressure rules out critical illness.”

Answer: C · “Use ABCDE; recognise shock and organ dysfunction early; resuscitate while diagnosing; identify the shock phenotype and surgical source; obtain timely haemorrhage control or source control; reassess response continuously; and escalate early.”

This is the practical framework. The sick surgical patient requires parallel processing: structured resuscitation, physiological interpretation, targeted investigation, definitive intervention, repeated reassessment, and multidisciplinary escalation.

  • SIRS: HR 110, RR 25, T 38.5, WBC 13,000 with normal BP → SIRS; HR is a SIRS criterion; T 38.4 + WBC 14,000 supports SIRS; organ dysfunction → "severe sepsis". 442 432 ×3 441 432 ×2

2. Shock phenotypes & haemodynamic support

Case 5 — Persistent shock after fluid: what next?

A septic postoperative patient receives 1.5 L balanced crystalloid. MAP rises from 58 to 67 mmHg, but there is persistent tachycardia, oliguria, mottling to the knees, and lactate 5.2 mmol/L. What is the most useful next haemodynamic assessment?

  • A. Measure central venous pressure and give fluid until CVP is 12 mmHg
  • B. Use a dynamic test of fluid responsiveness and assess cardiac function with focused echocardiography
  • C. Give repeated 1-L crystalloid boluses until the urine output improves
  • D. Start diuretics to treat presumed fluid overload
  • E. Wait for the next formal echocardiogram the following day

Answer: B · Use a dynamic test of fluid responsiveness and assess cardiac function with focused echocardiography

Persistent shock after initial resuscitation requires phenotyping. Dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness and focused echocardiography help distinguish persistent preload responsiveness, vasoplegia, ventricular dysfunction, tamponade, right-heart strain, or mixed shock. Static preload indices alone are unreliable.

  • Tachycardia + low urine output after sleeve gastrectomy → leak. 436

Case 7 — Hypotension and crackles after fluid

A 78-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease becomes hypotensive after 2 L crystalloid for presumed sepsis. He now has bilateral crackles, elevated JVP, cool peripheries, and persistent lactate elevation. Which is the best interpretation?

  • A. He definitely needs another 2 L crystalloid
  • B. He has simple hypovolaemia only
  • C. He may have mixed septic and cardiogenic shock
  • D. Raised JVP excludes shock
  • E. Sepsis is no longer possible because pulmonary oedema is present

Answer: C · He may have mixed septic and cardiogenic shock

Shock phenotypes frequently overlap. Sepsis can coexist with myocardial dysfunction, fluid overload, acute coronary syndrome, or pre-existing ventricular impairment. Further indiscriminate fluid may be harmful; use echocardiography, dynamic assessment, appropriate vasoactive support, and early critical-care input.

  • Fever, confusion, BP 80/50, lactate 4.5 → septic shock 441; flushed, hypotensive and confused POD 6 → septic shock. 430

Case 9 — Distributive or haemorrhagic?

A patient has shock after an emergency laparotomy. Which finding most strongly supports distributive rather than haemorrhagic shock at that moment?

  • A. Cold mottled skin and narrow pulse pressure
  • B. Rising drain output with falling haemoglobin
  • C. Warm peripheries with bounding pulses and low systemic vascular tone
  • D. Increasing abdominal girth with a falling haemoglobin
  • E. Positive FAST scan after trauma

Answer: C · Warm peripheries with bounding pulses and low systemic vascular tone

Early distributive shock can present with warm extremities, bounding pulses, and reduced vascular tone. However, surgical patients may have mixed shock; never use one sign alone to exclude haemorrhage or sepsis.

  • Septic shock = systemic vasodilation (↓ SVR), collapsed IVC, hyperdynamic LV; peripheral vasodilation; microcirculatory dysfunction. 442 432 ×5 431 ×2

Case 10 — Norepinephrine through a peripheral line

A patient with septic shock is receiving norepinephrine through a well-functioning peripheral IV while central access is being arranged. Which is the best principle?

  • A. Vasopressors must never be given peripherally
  • B. Norepinephrine should be withheld until central venous access is obtained
  • C. Timely vasopressor therapy should not be delayed solely for central access, provided the peripheral line is appropriate and closely monitored
  • D. Peripheral norepinephrine eliminates the need for ICU involvement
  • E. Central venous pressure should guide the norepinephrine dose

Answer: C · Timely vasopressor therapy should not be delayed solely for central access, provided the peripheral line is appropriate and closely monitored

In profound vasodilatory shock, delayed restoration of perfusion pressure may be harmful. A suitable proximal peripheral line can be used temporarily with close monitoring while central access and invasive monitoring are arranged.

  • Fastest access in an adult trauma with difficult IV access → intraosseous. 432 ×2

Case 14 — Septic shock with severe aortic stenosis

A patient with known severe aortic stenosis is septic and hypotensive. Which management principle is most important?

  • A. Give large, unmonitored fluid boluses until pulmonary oedema develops
  • B. Avoid all vasopressors
  • C. Maintain adequate coronary perfusion pressure while avoiding both severe tachycardia and fluid overload
  • D. Treat tachycardia with high-dose beta-blockade before stabilising blood pressure
  • E. Assume hypotension is due solely to sepsis

Answer: C · Maintain adequate coronary perfusion pressure while avoiding both severe tachycardia and fluid overload

Severe aortic stenosis limits the ability to increase cardiac output. Hypotension reduces coronary perfusion, while tachycardia reduces diastolic filling and coronary perfusion. Management requires careful haemodynamic support, cautious fluid strategy, vasopressors where appropriate, rhythm optimisation, and senior anaesthetic/ICU involvement.

Case 34 — Sepsis with severe heart failure: fluids

A patient with sepsis has HR 130/min, MAP 62 mmHg, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, and a history of severe heart failure. What is the best fluid strategy?

  • A. Give 30 mL/kg rapidly regardless of reassessment
  • B. Avoid all fluid because of heart failure
  • C. Give cautious, reassessed fluid challenges guided by perfusion and fluid responsiveness, with early vasopressor support if needed
  • D. Give diuretics immediately
  • E. Use CVP alone to determine volume status

Answer: C · Give cautious, reassessed fluid challenges guided by perfusion and fluid responsiveness, with early vasopressor support if needed

Pre-existing heart failure changes—but does not eliminate—the need for resuscitation. Use small reassessed boluses, dynamic testing, bedside echocardiography, lung ultrasound, and close monitoring. In severe vasoplegia, early vasopressor support may be preferable to indiscriminate fluid loading.

  • HR 160, BP 90/60 a day after lung resection → atrial fibrillation. 439

Case 35 — Oliguria with a blocked catheter

A patient is postoperative day 1 after laparotomy. They have oliguria, creatinine rising from 80 to 150 µmol/L, HR 110/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, and a blocked urinary catheter with a distended bladder on bedside scan. What is the next best step?

  • A. Diagnose intrinsic acute kidney injury and start dialysis
  • B. Give high-dose furosemide before checking the catheter
  • C. Restore catheter drainage, reassess urine output and physiology, while evaluating for concurrent hypoperfusion
  • D. Ignore the oliguria because postoperative AKI is inevitable
  • E. Remove the catheter and avoid further monitoring

Answer: C · Restore catheter drainage, reassess urine output and physiology, while evaluating for concurrent hypoperfusion

Always exclude post-renal obstruction and technical causes before attributing oliguria to intrinsic renal injury. However, a blocked catheter may coexist with shock or sepsis; reassess global perfusion and fluid status rather than stopping at the first abnormality.

3. Haemorrhage

Case 2 — Transient responder with a positive FAST

A 34-year-old man with blunt abdominal trauma has HR 132/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, cool peripheries, and a positive FAST examination. He transiently improves after a small blood-product bolus but becomes hypotensive again. What is the best next step?

  • A. CT angiography of the abdomen
  • B. Start norepinephrine and observe response
  • C. Immediate transfer to theatre for haemorrhage control
  • D. Give 2 L of crystalloid before further decisions
  • E. Repeat FAST in one hour

Answer: C · Immediate transfer to theatre for haemorrhage control

An unstable trauma patient with a positive FAST and transient response to resuscitation likely has ongoing intra-abdominal haemorrhage. The priority is definitive haemorrhage control, usually laparotomy. CT is for sufficiently stable or stabilised patients; vasopressors do not replace haemorrhage control.

  • Resuscitated trauma patient: class II hemorrhage = HR 100–120, normal SBP, RR 20–30 (BP 100/60, HR 110). 430
  • Trauma patient BP 88/56, HR 121, talking → 1 L bolus of RL 438 ×7; resuscitation fluid → Ringer's lactate. 441 434 ×2 431 ×3
  • Hyperchloremic acidosis after resuscitation → bolus Ringer's lactate. 430

Case 3 — Hypotension after lap chole, little in the drain

A 68-year-old woman develops hypotension 6 hours after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She has HR 120/min, BP 82/48 mmHg, cool extremities, haemoglobin 8.8 g/dL from 12.6 g/dL preoperatively, and increasing abdominal distension. Her drain contains only 30 mL of blood-stained fluid. What is the most likely explanation?

  • A. The drain output excludes clinically significant bleeding
  • B. The patient has opioid-related hypotension
  • C. She may have concealed intra-abdominal haemorrhage despite low drain output
  • D. She has distributive shock from early biliary sepsis
  • E. The haemoglobin fall is due to haemodilution only

Answer: C · She may have concealed intra-abdominal haemorrhage despite low drain output

Drains may not communicate with the bleeding compartment and can become blocked. Hypotension, tachycardia, falling haemoglobin, and abdominal distension should be treated as haemorrhage until proved otherwise. Resuscitate, crossmatch/activate blood products as appropriate, obtain urgent senior surgical and anaesthetic input, and move toward haemorrhage control.

  • Hypotension + bradycardia + warm extremities after trauma (spinal injury) → neurogenic shock 438 ×9 430; treat with IV fluids + vasopressors. 426
  • Warfarin with active bleeding and instability → stop warfarin, IV vitamin K + FFP (or PCC). 442
  • Unconscious trauma patient not moving limbs (possible C-spine) → open the airway with a jaw thrust (no head tilt) 438 ×3 432 ×3; stridor and SpO₂ 88% after a fall → in-line immobilisation + definitive airway. 438 ×6

Case 28 — Retroperitoneal bleed on anticoagulants

An elderly anticoagulated patient has abdominal pain, shock, and CT evidence of retroperitoneal haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate early management package?

  • A. Continue anticoagulation, give crystalloid, and repeat CT tomorrow
  • B. Resuscitate, reverse anticoagulation as appropriate, activate blood-product support, and arrange haemorrhage control with interventional radiology or surgery
  • C. Give antibiotics alone
  • D. Start therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin
  • E. Wait for the INR to correct spontaneously

Answer: B · Resuscitate, reverse anticoagulation as appropriate, activate blood-product support, and arrange haemorrhage control with interventional radiology or surgery

This is a haemorrhage-control problem. Address circulation, blood products, coagulation reversal tailored to the anticoagulant, warming, calcium, and rapid definitive control where needed.

Case 31 — Poor clotting after massive transfusion

A patient with haemorrhagic shock has received multiple units of packed red cells. They become hypotensive with poor clot formation at the operative field. Temperature is 34°C, pH 7.16, and ionised calcium is low. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

  • A. The only remaining problem is low haemoglobin
  • B. This is trauma-induced coagulopathy worsened by hypothermia, acidosis, and hypocalcaemia
  • C. More crystalloid is the principal treatment
  • D. Hypothermia is protective in haemorrhage
  • E. Calcium has no role in coagulation or cardiac function

Answer: B · This is trauma-induced coagulopathy worsened by hypothermia, acidosis, and hypocalcaemia

Major haemorrhage produces a self-perpetuating cycle of hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypocalcaemia. Management includes rapid haemorrhage control, warming, balanced blood products according to local protocol, calcium replacement, and minimisation of unnecessary crystalloid

  • Massive transfusion complications: hyperkalemia, citrate toxicity (hypocalcemia), hypothermia, coagulopathy. 431 ×2 431 ×3

Case 32 — Why limit crystalloid in bleeding trauma

A trauma patient has ongoing bleeding but is awake and has no traumatic brain injury. During transfer to theatre, their systolic BP is 85 mmHg. What is the rationale for avoiding large crystalloid volumes?

  • A. Crystalloid has no effect on intravascular volume
  • B. Excess crystalloid may dilute clotting factors, worsen hypothermia and acidosis, and dislodge forming clots
  • C. Crystalloid always causes renal failure
  • D. Blood products are contraindicated before crossmatch
  • E. Permissive hypotension is appropriate in all patients, including traumatic brain injury

Answer: B · Excess crystalloid may dilute clotting factors, worsen hypothermia and acidosis, and dislodge forming clots

Damage-control resuscitation minimises crystalloid, prioritises haemostatic blood-product resuscitation, and aims for early definitive haemorrhage control. Permissive hypotension is not suitable when traumatic brain injury or other conditions require adequate perfusion pressure

  • Anaphylaxis to IV contrast (bradycardia, hypotension) → intravascular volume redistribution (vasodilation, leak). 431 ×2
  • Conscious trauma patient, BP 75/45, on O₂ → next two large-bore IV lines. 431
  • Upper GI bleed (variceal or ulcer): airway first if GCS is low, then crystalloid resuscitation, then endoscopy. 438 ×3 438 ×5 431 430 430
  • Egyptian patient (old bilharziasis), hematemesis, HR 110, BP 100/65, ascites + splenomegaly (variceal bleed) → first IV fluid resuscitation. 429 Final
  • Excess opiates → high PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis). 431 ×3

4. Sepsis & source control

Case 6 — Perforated diverticulitis with shock

A patient with perforated diverticulitis has HR 125/min, BP 90/55 mmHg, lactate 5.0 mmol/L, diffuse peritonism, and free intraperitoneal air. After initial resuscitation and antibiotics, which action is most appropriate?

  • A. Delay surgery until the lactate normalises
  • B. Obtain serial abdominal radiographs for 24 hours
  • C. Proceed urgently to source control once initial resuscitation is underway
  • D. Manage non-operatively because antibiotics have been given
  • E. Wait for a CT-guided drain to become available

Answer: C · Proceed urgently to source control once initial resuscitation is underway

Generalised peritonitis with shock physiology requires urgent source control. Resuscitation should occur simultaneously, not sequentially as a prerequisite for prolonged delay. In abdominal sepsis, source control consists of controlling contamination, draining infected fluid, debriding non-viable tissue, and addressing the anatomical lesion.

  • Severe pancreatitis: generalized edema despite fluids → third-space losses. 438 ×3 432 ×4

Case 27 — Perforated peptic ulcer, now stable

A patient with perforated peptic ulcer has been resuscitated, given antibiotics and a proton-pump inhibitor, and is now more stable. Why is definitive source control still needed?

  • A. Antibiotics do not penetrate the peritoneal cavity
  • B. The perforation permits ongoing contamination and cannot be reliably treated with resuscitation alone in diffuse peritonitis
  • C. A normal lactate means surgery is unnecessary
  • D. Source control is only needed if cultures are positive
  • E. Surgical repair is solely for pain control

Answer: B · The perforation permits ongoing contamination and cannot be reliably treated with resuscitation alone in diffuse peritonitis

Resuscitation and antibiotics do not correct an ongoing anatomical leak. In diffuse peritonitis or persistent physiological compromise, operative or other definitive source control is required.

Case 21 — Anastomotic leak after colorectal resection

A 70-year-old patient is day 4 after colorectal resection. HR is 116/min, temperature 38.4°C, CRP is rising, abdominal pain is increasing, and drain output has become faeculent. CT shows a 6-cm pelvic collection with contrast extravasation near the anastomosis. The patient is normotensive after initial fluid. What is the best next step?

  • A. Oral antibiotics and repeat CT in one week
  • B. Remove the drain and discharge the patient
  • C. Urgent senior surgical review for source-control strategy; options may include drainage, diversion, or reoperation depending on stability and anatomy
  • D. Increase opioid analgesia and repeat CRP tomorrow
  • E. Give total parenteral nutrition as sole treatment

Answer: C · Urgent senior surgical review for source-control strategy; options may include drainage, diversion, or reoperation depending on stability and anatomy

This is an anastomotic leak with ongoing contamination. Source control is the priority; the method depends on clinical stability, degree of peritonitis, accessible collection, anastomotic anatomy, and local expertise. Antibiotics are necessary but insufficient if contamination remains uncontrolled.

Case 22 — Acute mesenteric ischaemia with peritonism

A patient with acute mesenteric ischaemia has severe pain, lactate 6.5 mmol/L, metabolic acidosis, and peritonism. Which approach is most appropriate?

  • A. Treat with analgesia and reassess lactate in 12 hours
  • B. Prioritise urgent surgical/vascular assessment and revascularisation or laparotomy according to anatomy and bowel viability
  • C. Delay intervention until bowel necrosis is visible on plain radiography
  • D. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics only
  • E. Start oral anticoagulation and discharge if pain improves

Answer: B · Prioritise urgent surgical/vascular assessment and revascularisation or laparotomy according to anatomy and bowel viability

Peritonism and acidosis suggest advanced disease and potential bowel necrosis. This requires immediate specialist escalation, resuscitation, antimicrobials where appropriate, anticoagulation when indicated and safe, and urgent revascularisation and/or laparotomy.

  • Pneumonia patient on 3 vasopressors who becomes anuric → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI) (keyed). 439
  • ICU septic shock + sudden abdominal pain, distension, lactic acidosis → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. 442 Final

Case 23 — Necrotising pancreatitis deteriorating

A patient with severe pancreatitis develops increasing oxygen requirements, oliguria, abdominal distension, and a rising lactate. CT shows pancreatic necrosis but no gas in collections. What is the best immediate interpretation?

  • A. Necrosis automatically requires immediate pancreatic debridement
  • B. The patient requires urgent reassessment for organ failure and intra-abdominal hypertension; intervention should be driven by infection, complications, and physiology
  • C. Antibiotics are mandatory for all sterile necrosis
  • D. The CT excludes abdominal compartment syndrome
  • E. The patient can be managed without critical-care involvement

Answer: B · The patient requires urgent reassessment for organ failure and intra-abdominal hypertension; intervention should be driven by infection, complications, and physiology

Necrotising pancreatitis is managed according to physiology and complications. Sterile necrosis does not automatically require intervention. Deterioration should prompt assessment for organ failure, abdominal compartment syndrome, infection, bleeding, ischaemia, and need for ICU-level support.

  • The SIRS-in-ICU question keyed gastroduodenal (stress) ulcer as the supporting finding. 441
  • Long critical illness (necrotizing pancreatitis on ventilator/inotropes): stress response → insulin resistance and ↑ glucagon (keys differ: 434 = glucagon, 433 = insulin). 434 433
  • VAP prevention → daily sedation hold / extubation trials 439; most common ICU infection in burns → VAP. 442
  • Intra-abdominal pressure 32 mmHg with oliguria and rising ventilatory pressures → abdominal compartment syndrome. 442

Case 24 — Small-bowel obstruction turning toxic

A patient with small-bowel obstruction develops persistent pain, tachycardia, fever, metabolic acidosis, and localised peritonism. What complication should be presumed until excluded?

  • A. Simple adhesive obstruction resolving spontaneously
  • B. Strangulation with bowel ischaemia
  • C. Functional constipation
  • D. Viral gastroenteritis
  • E. Uncomplicated postoperative ileus

Answer: B · Strangulation with bowel ischaemia

Pain out of proportion or becoming continuous, systemic toxicity, acidosis, peritonism, and worsening physiology suggest strangulation and bowel ischaemia. This requires urgent surgical review and usually operative management; do not delay for prolonged conservative therapy.

Case 25 — Severe ascending cholangitis

A patient has severe biliary sepsis from ascending cholangitis: fever, jaundice, hypotension, confusion, bilirubin elevation, and a dilated common bile duct. What is the key definitive intervention after initial resuscitation and antibiotics?

  • A. Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 6 weeks only
  • B. Urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP where feasible
  • C. Oral analgesia and discharge
  • D. Routine appendicectomy
  • E. Observation until liver enzymes normalise

Answer: B · Urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP where feasible

Severe cholangitis requires resuscitation, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and biliary drainage. In a patient with septic shock or persistent obstruction, source control cannot be deferred simply because antibiotics have been started.

Case 26 — Septic shock despite a drain

A postoperative patient has persistent septic shock after broad-spectrum antibiotics and CT-guided drainage of a pelvic collection. Repeat imaging shows multiple undrained locules and free intraperitoneal fluid. What is the most appropriate next principle?

  • A. Persist with the same treatment because the drain has been placed
  • B. Reassess adequacy of source control and consider additional drainage or operative re-exploration
  • C. Stop antibiotics because they have failed
  • D. Treat only the lactate value
  • E. Remove all drains to reduce infection risk

Answer: B · Reassess adequacy of source control and consider additional drainage or operative re-exploration

Failure to improve should trigger a source-control review. Drain placement is not synonymous with adequate drainage. Consider residual collections, inaccessible locules, ongoing leak, necrotic tissue, incorrect diagnosis, resistant organisms, or another source.

Case 30 — Drain or laparotomy?

Which situation most strongly supports percutaneous drainage rather than immediate laparotomy for postoperative intra-abdominal sepsis?

  • A. Diffuse peritonitis with refractory septic shock
  • B. A well-defined, accessible localised abscess in a haemodynamically stable patient without generalised peritonitis
  • C. Free perforation with faeculent peritonitis
  • D. Ongoing haemorrhage with instability
  • E. Suspected bowel ischaemia with peritonism

Answer: B · A well-defined, accessible localised abscess in a haemodynamically stable patient without generalised peritonitis

Image-guided drainage is often effective for a localised, accessible collection in a stable patient. Diffuse peritonitis, uncontrolled contamination, bowel ischaemia, or severe physiological deterioration generally requires urgent operative source control.

  • Fever, hiccups and tachycardia after sleeve gastrectomy → CT for leak/abscess. 437

5. Respiratory deterioration & the airway

Case 11 — Drowsy, slow breathing after opioids

A patient is postoperative day 1 after upper abdominal surgery. They are drowsy, RR 8/min, PCO₂ 9.0 kPa, pH 7.21, oxygen saturation 89% on 2 L/min oxygen, and have received repeated opioid boluses. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

  • A. Increase opioid dosing because splinting is likely
  • B. Treat only with supplemental oxygen
  • C. Support airway and ventilation, stop further sedatives/opioids, and use titrated naloxone if opioid toxicity is likely
  • D. Arrange CT pulmonary angiography before intervening
  • E. Start antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia without airway assessment

Answer: C · Support airway and ventilation, stop further sedatives/opioids, and use titrated naloxone if opioid toxicity is likely

This is hypercapnic ventilatory failure, likely opioid related. Oxygen alone may improve saturation while worsening unrecognised hypercapnia. Priorities are airway assessment, ventilatory support, reversal where appropriate, close monitoring, and management of pain with a safer multimodal strategy once stabilised.

  • Drowsy in recovery with SpO₂ 90% and normal pulse/BP → respiratory failure (residual anaesthetic/opioids). 430

Case 15 — Tiring patient with a rising PCO₂

A patient with abdominal sepsis is becoming progressively fatigued. RR is 38/min, oxygen saturation 92% on high-flow oxygen, PCO₂ rises from 4.2 to 5.8 kPa, and mental status deteriorates. What is the best interpretation?

  • A. Improved ventilation because PCO₂ is rising
  • B. Impending ventilatory failure despite an initially low PCO₂ from tachypnoea
  • C. Simple anxiety
  • D. Isolated metabolic alkalosis
  • E. Adequate compensation that needs no escalation

Answer: B · Impending ventilatory failure despite an initially low PCO₂ from tachypnoea

In severe illness, a patient may initially maintain or lower PCO₂ through increased respiratory effort. A subsequent rising PCO₂, worsening mental state, and exhaustion signal failing ventilation. Escalate early for airway and ventilatory support.

  • Emphysema + hematemesis, pH 7.23, PO₂ 42, PCO₂ 75, confused → intubate and ventilate (426 key: correct hypoxia with O₂). 430 ×2 426

Case 12 — Collapse after subclavian line insertion

A patient becomes acutely hypoxaemic and hypotensive shortly after subclavian central venous catheter insertion. There is unilateral absent breath sound and distended neck veins. Which action should occur before chest radiography?

  • B. Immediate decompression for presumed tension pneumothorax
  • C. Give IV furosemide
  • D. Insert a nasogastric tube
  • E. Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics

Answer: B · Immediate decompression for presumed tension pneumothorax

This is tension pneumothorax until proved otherwise. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression, followed by definitive pleural drainage. Imaging must not delay treatment in an unstable patient.

  • Tamponade vs tension pneumothorax: the differentiating sign is breath sounds (both have raised JVP and hypotension). 438 ×3

Case 20 — Frothy sputum and B-lines

A postoperative patient has acute dyspnoea, frothy sputum, diffuse crackles, hypertension, and ultrasound B-lines. What is the most likely primary physiology?

  • B. Tension pneumothorax
  • C. Haemorrhagic shock
  • D. Complete airway obstruction
  • E. Isolated metabolic acidosis

Answer: A · Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema

The clinical pattern is consistent with acute pulmonary oedema. Management depends on the cause—acute LV dysfunction, hypertensive crisis, fluid overload, valvular pathology, or arrhythmia—and includes oxygen/ventilatory support, haemodynamic assessment, and cause-directed treatment.

  • Primary survey order: Airway with C-spine precautions → Breathing → Circulation. 430

Case 16 — Induction in a shocked, vomiting patient

A patient with peritonitis requires emergency laparotomy. They are hypotensive, tachycardic, acidotic, and actively vomiting. What is the key anaesthetic concern during induction?

  • B. Cardiovascular collapse from induction in a severely under-resuscitated patient, plus aspiration risk
  • C. Delayed wound healing only
  • D. Isolated postoperative nausea
  • E. Development of chronic pain syndrome

Answer: B · Cardiovascular collapse from induction in a severely under-resuscitated patient, plus aspiration risk

Induction and positive-pressure ventilation can abruptly reduce venous return and sympathetic tone, precipitating collapse in shock. The patient also has a full stomach and aspiration risk. Resuscitation, blood products/vasopressors, skilled airway planning, and clear surgeon–anaesthetist communication are essential.

  • Anterior MI with BP 80/50 (cardiogenic shock) → normal intravascular volume 431 ×3; chest pain + hypotension POD 1 → cardiogenic shock. 430
  • Collapse in recovery 1 h after appendectomy → hypovolemic shock (bleeding) 431 ×3; bleeding, aspiration and PE are causes — wound abscess is NOT (too early). 426

Case 17 — Hypotension right after intubation

A patient becomes hypotensive immediately after intubation for septic shock. Which explanation is most likely?

  • A. The sepsis has resolved
  • B. Loss of sympathetic tone, induction-related vasodilatation, and reduced venous return from positive-pressure ventilation
  • C. The blood pressure monitor is always incorrect after intubation
  • D. Antibiotics are causing immediate vasoconstriction
  • E. The endotracheal tube has improved cardiac output

Answer: B · Loss of sympathetic tone, induction-related vasodilatation, and reduced venous return from positive-pressure ventilation

Peri-intubation hypotension is common in critically ill patients. Anticipate it by optimising intravascular status where appropriate, preparing vasopressors, considering reduced induction doses, using experienced airway personnel, and checking for other causes such as tension pneumothorax or occult haemorrhage.

  • Stab wound, unconscious, BP 70/40 (class IV) → first endotracheal intubation (airway). 432 ×4
  • GCS ≤ 8 → intubate (GCS 6 or 7 trauma patient). 431 439

6. Pulmonary embolism

Case 13 — Dilated right ventricle on day 5

A 64-year-old patient develops sudden hypoxaemia and hypotension on postoperative day 5. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates a dilated right ventricle with septal flattening. Which diagnosis is most likely?

  • A. Left ventricular failure from fluid overload
  • B. Acute pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock
  • C. Isolated hypovolaemia
  • D. Pericarditis without haemodynamic consequence
  • E. Tension pneumoperitoneum

Answer: B · Acute pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock

Acute right ventricular dilatation and septal flattening in an appropriate clinical context raise concern for acute pulmonary embolism with right-heart strain. Consider other causes of acute pulmonary hypertension or RV failure, but urgently escalate because management may include anticoagulation, reperfusion therapy, and critical-care support depending on bleeding risk and haemodynamic status.

  • Hard to bag, reduced air entry left, trachea to the right → needle decompression, left 2nd intercostal space. 430

Case 18 — Stable, PE likely: which test?

A patient after major abdominal surgery has tachycardia, hypoxaemia, pleuritic chest pain, and a low-grade fever. Which is the best next diagnostic step if they are haemodynamically stable and pulmonary embolism is clinically likely?

  • A. D-dimer only
  • B. CT pulmonary angiography, if no contraindication
  • C. Chest physiotherapy only
  • D. Start antibiotics and reassess in 24 hours
  • E. Routine abdominal ultrasound

Answer: B · CT pulmonary angiography, if no contraindication

In a stable patient with a high clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism, CT pulmonary angiography is usually the definitive diagnostic test. A D-dimer has limited utility in many postoperative inpatients because it is frequently elevated.

  • Fever, chest tightness, pain at the infusion site, hypotension, dark urine during transfusion → acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. 437 ×4 431 ×2
  • Post-op chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension, normal ECG/enzymes (POD 5 after APR) → CT chest (CTPA) for PE 438 ×9; massive PE with BP responding to fluid → LMWH (keyed). 430

Case 19 — PE with hypotension and RV strain

A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism is hypotensive and has echocardiographic evidence of right ventricular strain. What should be done while definitive imaging and treatment decisions are being arranged?

  • A. Give large-volume crystalloid until blood pressure normalises
  • B. Begin supportive resuscitation, obtain immediate senior multidisciplinary input, and assess bleeding risk for reperfusion strategy
  • C. Delay all treatment until CT confirms embolism
  • D. Give diuretics only
  • E. Send the patient to the ward for observation

Answer: B · Begin supportive resuscitation, obtain immediate senior multidisciplinary input, and assess bleeding risk for reperfusion strategy

High-risk pulmonary embolism may cause obstructive shock and requires urgent multidisciplinary management. Excessive fluid can worsen RV dilatation; carefully titrated haemodynamic support and consideration of reperfusion are needed.

7. Abdominal compartment syndrome & damage control

Case 8 — Tense abdomen in bowel obstruction

A patient with bowel obstruction becomes increasingly distressed, tachycardic, and hypotensive. Their abdomen is tense and markedly distended. They have worsening oliguria and increasing ventilatory pressures after intubation. What complication should be strongly considered?

  • A. Isolated postoperative ileus
  • B. Abdominal compartment syndrome
  • C. Uncomplicated opioid withdrawal
  • D. Acute viral gastroenteritis
  • E. Neurogenic shock

Answer: B · Abdominal compartment syndrome

A tense distended abdomen with new organ dysfunction—renal impairment, worsening respiratory mechanics, impaired venous return, and shock—suggests intra-abdominal hypertension/abdominal compartment syndrome. Urgent escalation, measurement of intra-abdominal pressure where available, optimisation of abdominal wall compliance, decompression, and consideration of surgical decompression are required.

  • Same picture but with tachycardia (HR 120) — the compilers note this doesn't fit neurogenic shock (which has bradycardia). 432

Case 29 — When to relook after damage control

A patient after damage-control laparotomy is in ICU with temporary abdominal closure. Which clinical change should most strongly trigger concern for ongoing intra-abdominal pathology requiring relook?

  • A. Gradual improvement in lactate and vasopressor requirement
  • B. Falling ventilatory pressures and improving urine output
  • C. Worsening acidosis, rising lactate, escalating vasopressor needs, and increasing abdominal effluent
  • D. A mildly elevated CRP alone
  • E. Return of bowel sounds

Answer: C · Worsening acidosis, rising lactate, escalating vasopressor needs, and increasing abdominal effluent

Deteriorating physiology after damage-control surgery may indicate ongoing bleeding, uncontrolled contamination, bowel ischaemia, or abdominal compartment pathology. The patient needs immediate multidisciplinary reassessment and consideration of earlier relook surgery.

Case 45 — Tense abdomen after liver packing

A 50-year-old man is in ICU after damage-control laparotomy for grade IV liver injury. Packing was performed and temporary abdominal closure applied. He initially stabilised, but four hours later he develops rising vasopressor requirements, lactate increases from 4.0 to 8.1 mmol/L, pH falls to 7.18, urine output falls to 5 mL/hour, and peak airway pressures increase substantially. His abdomen appears progressively tense beneath the temporary closure. Drain output is minimal. Focused echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic, underfilled left ventricle without pericardial effusion or right-ventricular strain. What is the most likely immediate explanation and priority action?

  • A. Cardiogenic shock; begin inotropic therapy
  • B. Tension pneumothorax; perform immediate thoracic decompression
  • C. Abdominal compartment syndrome; urgently assess intra-abdominal pressure and prepare for decompression/relook laparotomy
  • D. Septic shock from established intra-abdominal infection; wait for cultures before changing management
  • E. Occult cerebral herniation; give hypertonic saline

Answer: C · Abdominal compartment syndrome; urgently assess intra-abdominal pressure and prepare for decompression/relook laparotomy

The combination of a tense abdomen, rapidly worsening renal function, rising airway pressures, escalating shock, deteriorating acidosis, and an underfilled hyperdynamic ventricle suggests impaired venous return and organ perfusion from abdominal compartment syndrome. Minimal drain output does not exclude intra-abdominal pressure elevation. Measurement of intra-abdominal pressure can support the diagnosis, but an unstable patient with compelling physiology requires immediate senior surgical and ICU action, including urgent decompression or relook laparotomy when indicated.

8. Complex trauma cases

Case 41 — Pelvic gunshot wounds, negative FAST

A 27-year-old man sustains multiple pelvic gunshot wounds. On arrival he has HR 142/min, BP 72/40 mmHg, temperature 34.1°C, pH 7.12, lactate 9.0 mmol/L, and a pelvic binder is correctly positioned. FAST is negative. Chest examination is normal. His abdomen is soft but unreliable because he is obtunded. Massive transfusion is underway. After receiving 4 units of packed red cells and 4 units of plasma, he remains profoundly hypotensive. Pelvic radiograph shows an unstable pelvic ring injury. What is the most appropriate next haemorrhage-control strategy?

  • A. CT angiography to identify the precise bleeding vessel before intervention
  • B. Remove the pelvic binder to permit a more accurate abdominal examination
  • C. Immediate preperitoneal pelvic packing with pelvic stabilisation, with angioembolisation considered for persistent arterial bleeding
  • D. Exploratory laparotomy as the sole first procedure because FAST can miss pelvic haemorrhage
  • E. Give further crystalloid until systolic blood pressure exceeds 120 mmHg

Answer: C · Immediate preperitoneal pelvic packing with pelvic stabilisation, with angioembolisation considered for persistent arterial bleeding

This patient has exsanguinating pelvic trauma. A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding. In a profoundly unstable patient, haemorrhage control must not be delayed for CT. Mechanical stabilisation with a correctly positioned binder plus rapid preperitoneal pelvic packing addresses major venous and cancellous-bone bleeding; angioembolisation is valuable for persistent arterial bleeding after initial stabilisation. Laparotomy can worsen pelvic tamponade if it is performed without a clear intraperitoneal indication.

  • Gram-negative bacteremia after splenic rupture + transfusion → bacterial translocation from the bowel. 432 ×2

Case 42 — Subdural haematoma plus pelvic bleeding

A 34-year-old man is intubated after a high-speed road traffic collision. CT head demonstrates an acute subdural haematoma with 7-mm midline shift. He also has an unstable pelvic fracture and ongoing haemorrhagic shock. Current observations: BP 82/46 mmHg, HR 132/min, temperature 35°C, PaO₂ 11 kPa on FIO₂ 0.60, PaCO₂ 3.4 kPa, and pupils are unequal. Which management principle is most appropriate?

  • A. Accept permissive hypotension with systolic BP around 80–90 mmHg until pelvic bleeding is controlled
  • B. Maintain prolonged profound hyperventilation with PaCO₂ below 3.5 kPa to control intracranial pressure
  • C. Prioritise prevention of secondary brain injury by avoiding hypoxaemia and hypotension, while using damage-control haemorrhage management
  • D. Delay blood products because correction of coagulopathy may worsen the intracranial haematoma
  • E. Give repeated mannitol doses routinely until the pupils become symmetrical

Answer: C · Prioritise prevention of secondary brain injury by avoiding hypoxaemia and hypotension, while using damage-control haemorrhage management

This is combined TBI and haemorrhagic shock. Unlike isolated penetrating torso trauma, permissive hypotension is generally inappropriate in significant TBI because cerebral perfusion must be protected. Prevent hypoxaemia, hypotension, hypothermia, and coagulopathy while achieving rapid haemorrhage control. Brief controlled hyperventilation can be a temporising manoeuvre in impending herniation, but routine or prolonged severe hypocapnia risks cerebral ischaemia. Hyperosmolar therapy is used intermittently for intracranial-pressure elevation or herniation risk, not as an automatic repeated routine treatment

  • Bleeding from cannula sites, prolonged PT/PTT, low platelets, high degradation products → DIC → D-dimer. 438 ×7

Case 43 — Ongoing oozing after massive transfusion

A 43-year-old woman undergoes damage-control laparotomy after blunt polytrauma with liver injury and pelvic fractures. She has received 10 units of packed red cells, 8 units of plasma, and 2 adult doses of platelets. Surgical packing is in place, but diffuse microvascular bleeding continues.

  • Temperature: 35.0°C
  • pH: 7.24
  • Ionised calcium: 0.88 mmol/L
  • Platelet count: 118 × 10⁹/L
  • INR: 1.4
  • Clauss fibrinogen: 0.9 g/L
  • Viscoelastic test: low clot amplitude consistent with functional fibrinogen deficit; no significant hyperfibrinolysis

Which is the best targeted next haemostatic intervention?

  • A. Give additional packed red cells only because the haemoglobin is 85 g/L
  • B. Give fibrinogen replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, correct hypocalcaemia, and actively rewarm
  • C. Give tranexamic acid only after waiting for repeat viscoelastic testing
  • D. Give therapeutic-dose heparin because fibrinogen replacement increases thrombosis risk
  • E. Give 2 L normal saline to improve microcirculatory flow

Answer: B · Give fibrinogen replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, correct hypocalcaemia, and actively rewarm

The key haemostatic deficit is hypofibrinogenaemia with a viscoelastic functional fibrinogen deficit. Fibrinogen is often the first coagulation factor to fall to critically low levels in major haemorrhage. Replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is indicated in significant bleeding with fibrinogen ≤1.5 g/L or a functional fibrinogen deficit on viscoelastic testing. Simultaneously correct ionised hypocalcaemia and hypothermia, both of which impair coagulation and cardiovascular function. TXA should be administered early in an eligible bleeding trauma patient—ideally within three hours of injury—and should not wait for viscoelastic results, but the test here does not show hyperfibrinolysis as the dominant current deficit

  • Massive transfusion ratio PRBC : plasma : platelets = 1 : 1 : 1. 442
  • Oozing from lines after 6 units, low platelets, prolonged PT/PTT → give FFP next. 441 ×2

Case 44 — Raised ICP despite basic measures

A 23-year-old patient with severe diffuse traumatic brain injury has an intraparenchymal ICP monitor. He is sedated, ventilated, normothermic, and has had a stable repeat CT head. ICP has now remained at 28–30 mmHg for 15 minutes despite head elevation, neutral neck position, adequate analgesia/sedation, and correction of hypoxaemia. MAP is 82 mmHg and PaCO₂ is 5.0 kPa. Which is the best next step?

  • A. Institute routine sustained hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 2.5 kPa for the next 24 hours
  • B. Give intermittent hyperosmolar therapy and reassess ICP, serum sodium/osmolality, haemodynamics, and neurological status
  • C. Lower MAP deliberately to reduce cerebral oedema
  • D. Stop sedation to permit more accurate neurological examination
  • E. Give hypotonic maintenance fluid to correct presumed intracellular dehydration

Answer: B · Give intermittent hyperosmolar therapy and reassess ICP, serum sodium/osmolality, haemodynamics, and neurological status

Sustained intracranial hypertension despite basic measures warrants escalation with intermittent hyperosmolar therapy—using local protocol and appropriate monitoring—while ensuring cerebral perfusion and reassessing for reversible contributors, including seizures, fever, ventilator dyssynchrony, obstruction to venous drainage, and evolving structural pathology. Prolonged prophylactic severe hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow and is not recommended; brief hyperventilation is reserved as a rescue manoeuvre in impending herniation while definitive treatment is arranged. Hyperosmolar therapy should be delivered for ICP elevation, not on an automatic schedule.

Shock

Hypovolemic shock:
  • Hypovolemic shock occurs due to inadequate circulating blood volume, leading to decreased organ perfusion and oxygen delivery.
  • Causes include:
  • Bleeding (most common cause)
  • Severe vomiting or diarrhea
  • Fluid sequestration in the gut (e.g., bowel obstruction, burns)
Physiologic Compensation Mechanisms

The body compensates for hypovolemia through the adrenergic nervous system, which:

1. Constricts veins & venules, shifting blood toward the heart.

2. Constricts arterioles in non-essential organs (skin, muscle, gut, liver),

  • preserving blood flow to the brain & heart.

3. Increases heart rate & contractility to improve cardiac output.

4. Stimulates sodium & water retention via the renin-angiotensin-

  • aldosterone system and vasopressin release, helping to restore blood
  • volume.
Signs & Symptoms of Hypovolemic Shock
  • Early Signs:
  • Cool skin, delayed capillary refill (most sensitive early sign).
  • Difficult IV access due to vasoconstriction.
  • Orthostatic hypotension (SBP drop >20 mmHg or DBP drop >10 mmHg upon standing).
  • Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, <1 mL/kg/h in children, <2 mL/kg/h in infants).
  • Moderate Shock (20–30% blood loss):
  • Thirst & hypotension (even in supine position).
  • Metabolic acidosis due to anaerobic metabolism.
  • Severe Shock (>30% blood loss):
  • Profound hypotension and altered mental status (agitation, confusion, lethargy).
  • Myocardial ischemia (ST-T segment changes, arrhythmias).
  • Metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis post-resuscitation).
Diagnostic Pitfalls
  • Normal blood pressure does NOT rule out shock.
  • Heart rate is unreliable (some patients may have normal HR or even bradycardia in severe cases).
  • Mental status changes can mimic intoxication (shock must be ruled out before assuming drug/alcohol intoxication).
  • Cutaneous vasoconstriction may be masked by alcohol, vasodilators, or sedatives.
Laboratory & Monitoring Clues
  • Hematocrit falls within minutes if IV fluids are given, but may take hours without fluids.
  • A Hct drop of 3–4% suggests ~10% blood loss, while 6–8% suggests ~20% blood loss (~1 L in adults).
  • Bladder catheterization is essential to monitor urine output.

Management

A. Airway and Ventilation
  • Priority: Secure the airway immediately, especially in severe shock.
  • Preemptive Intubation & Mechanical Ventilation:
  • Ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation.
  • Prevents emergency intubation under unstable conditions.
  • Volume-Control Ventilation: Preferred in initial resuscitation.
  • Risks of Positive-Pressure Ventilation in Hypovolemia:
  • Compresses vena cava → Reduces venous return → Worsens hypotension.
  • Increases pulmonary vascular resistance → Impairs right heart function.
  • Reduces left atrial filling → Limits cardiac output.
  • Can lead to cardiovascular collapse if intubation is performed without fluid resuscitation.
  • Preparation for Possible Collapse: In emergency settings, teams must anticipate and prepare for sudden deterioration upon intubation.
B. Bleeding Control
1. External Bleeding:
  • Direct Pressure is the first step.
  • Tourniquets for extremity bleeding (safe for ≤2 hours).
  • Hemostatic Agents (commercially available, FDA-approved).
2. Internal Bleeding:
  • Chest Bleeding: Place a chest tube to drain blood, re-expand the lung, and monitor for ongoing hemorrhage.
  • Pelvic Fracture: Apply a pelvic binder; definitive control via angiographic embolization or surgery.
  • Long-Bone Fractures: Immobilization reduces further bleeding.
  • Abdominal or Thoracic Bleeding: Immediate surgical intervention is required.
3. Avoid Blind Clamping:
  • Risks: Can injure vessels and cause further bleeding.
C. Initial Fluid Resuscitation
1. Vascular Access
  • Large-bore IV access (16G or larger) via:
  • Peripheral veins (upper extremities)
  • Central veins (jugular, subclavian, femoral) with ultrasound guidance
  • Saphenous vein cutdown
  • Intraosseous (sternum, tibia, humerus) if IV access fails
2. Crystalloid Resuscitation (1-2 L Bolus Initially)
  • Options:
  • Normal saline (NS) – Preferred if pH > 7.2.
  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) – Used if severe acidosis (pH < 7.2) due to buffering effects.
  • Avoid LR in liver disease (inadequate lactate metabolism).
  • Caution:
  • Excess crystalloids can lead to dilutional coagulopathy and tissue edema.
  • If no response after 1-2 L of crystalloids, initiate blood transfusion.
D. Blood Product Transfusion
1. Indications for PRBC Transfusion:
  • >1.5 L blood loss (~30% of blood volume lost)
  • Earlier transfusion if:
  • Ongoing bleeding.
  • Preexisting coronary artery disease.
2. Emergency Transfusion Protocols:
  • Unmatched Type-O PRBCs: Used initially.
  • Rh-positive PRBCs for men and postmenopausal women.
  • Rh-negative PRBCs for women of childbearing age.
  • Type-Specific Blood: Can be given within 10 minutes.
3. Massive Transfusion Protocol (≥6 PRBCs Given):
  • 1:1:1 Ratio of PRBCs, Plasma, and Platelets
  • Prevents dilutional coagulopathy.
  • Improves oxygen delivery & hemostasis.
  • Avoids excessive crystalloid infusion.
E. Goals of Fluid Resuscitation
  • Avoid excessive fluids: Over-resuscitation leads to tissue edema, impairing organ function and wound healing.
  • Avoid under-resuscitation: Inadequate resuscitation increases the risk of multi-organ failure.
  • Targeted Resuscitation Goals:
  • Systolic BP of 80 mmHg (radial pulse present) until bleeding is controlled.
  • Systolic BP of 90 mmHg post-bleeding control.
  • Higher BP targets for elderly patients to ensure brain and cardiac perfusion.
  • Clinical indicators of adequate resuscitation:
  • Improved skin perfusion (warm, rapid capillary refill).
  • Urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults, >1 mL/kg/hr in children.
  • Improved mental status.
  • Normalization of acid-base balance (resolving metabolic acidosis).
  • Pitfalls:
  • BP alone is not a reliable marker due to compensatory vasoconstriction.
  • Ethanol or sedatives may interfere with compensatory responses.
  • Pain-induced hypertension should not be mistaken for normovolemia.
F. Correction of Coagulation Abnormalities
  • Trauma and sepsis often lead to coagulopathy with:
  • Prolonged clotting times (PT, aPTT).
  • Low platelets and fibrinogen.
  • Elevated fibrin degradation products.
  • Treatment strategies:
  • Plasma (FFP or pre-thawed plasma) for low clotting factors.
  • Platelets for counts <50,000 in active bleeding or <100,000 in head trauma.
  • Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC):
    • Rapidly reverses warfarin-related coagulopathy.
    • Reduces need for high-volume plasma transfusions.
  • Tranexamic Acid (TXA):
    • Prevents excessive fibrinolysis.
    • Effective if given within 3 hours of hemorrhage.
    • Thromboelastography (TEG) can guide TXA use.
  • Prehospital Plasma (PAMPer Trial):
  • ~10% mortality reduction in hemorrhagic shock patients.
  • Plasma use before hospital arrival improves survival.
G. Hypothermia: Prevention & Treatment
  • Hypothermia worsens coagulopathy → Increased bleeding risk.
  • Causes:
  • Blood loss → Reduced metabolic heat production.
  • Cold IV fluids and blood products.
  • Environmental exposure (trauma, surgery).
  • Preventive Strategies:
  • Keep operating room & resuscitation areas warm.
  • Use warmed IV fluids and blood products.
  • Minimize skin exposure during resuscitation.
  • Apply forced-air warming blankets (e.g., Bair Hugger).
  • Active Rewarming Methods:
  • Forced-air warming devices (most effective).
  • Heated IV fluids/blood products.
  • Warm blankets and head coverings.
  • Core warming via heated humidified oxygen.
  • Extracorporeal warming may be required for severe hypothermia (<32°C).
H. Modalities to Avoid
1. Colloids (e.g., Hetastarch, Dextran, Albumin)
  • No proven benefit over crystalloids.
  • Increase cost without improving survival.
  • May cause renal dysfunction and coagulopathy (Hetastarch).
  • Used only in mass casualty or battlefield scenarios when crystalloid volume is limited.
2. Vasopressors in Hypovolemia
  • Should NOT be used in hemorrhagic shock unless necessary.
  • Risk of ischemic complications:
  • Gut necrosis.
  • Limb ischemia and gangrene.
  • Acute kidney injury.
  • Liver failure.
  • Exception:
  • Temporary use in refractory shock while initiating aggressive volume resuscitation.
Cardiac Compressive (Obstructive) Shock:

Cardiac compressive shock occurs when external pressure on the heart or great veins impairs venous return and cardiac output. Common causes include:

1. Pericardial Tamponade
  • Fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac compresses the heart.
  • Beck's Triad:
    • Hypotension
    • Distended neck veins (JVD)
    • Muffled heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus: Decrease in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration (key diagnostic feature).
  • ECG: Electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude).

2. Tension Pneumothorax

  • Air trapped in the pleural space creates positive pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting mediastinal structures.
  • Signs:
    • Tracheal deviation (away from affected side)
    • Absent breath sounds on affected side
    • JVD and hypotension
  • CXR: Mediastinal shift and lung collapse.

3. Massive Hemothorax

  • Accumulation of blood (>1.5 L) in the pleural cavity impairs cardiac filling.
  • Signs:
    • Shock + Absent breath sounds + Dullness to percussion
    • JVD may be present in non-hypovolemic patients.
  • CXR: Large radio-opaque hemothorax.

4. Diaphragmatic Rupture with Herniation

  • Abdominal organs move into the thoracic cavity, compressing the heart.
  • Signs:
    • Dyspnea, bowel sounds in chest, epigastric pain.
  • CXR: Bowel loops in thorax, elevated hemidiaphragm.

5. Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS)

  • Severe intra-abdominal hypertension (>20 mmHg) compresses the IVC, reducing venous return and cardiac output.
  • Signs:
    • Tense, distended abdomen
    • Oliguria and high peak airway pressures (if ventilated)
  • Measurement: Bladder pressure (>20 mmHg) confirms ACS.
Treatment
1. Immediate Fluid Resuscitation (Bridging Strategy)
  • Bolus of IV fluids to improve venous return and transiently relieve compression.
  • Avoid excessive fluids to prevent worsening cardiac dysfunction.
2. Definitive Mechanical Correction
  • Pericardial Tamponade → Pericardiocentesis or Surgical Pericardial Window
  • US-guided pericardiocentesis is first-line for unstable patients.
  • Pericardial window in trauma or recurrent cases.
  • Tension Pneumothorax → Needle Decompression & Chest Tube
  • Needle decompression: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (quickest).
  • Chest tube insertion: 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line.
  • Massive Hemothorax → Tube Thoracostomy & Surgery
  • Chest tube drainage (if >1.5 L or >200 mL/hr, immediate surgery needed).
  • Diaphragmatic Herniation → Urgent Surgery
  • Laparotomy or thoracotomy for visceral reduction and diaphragm repair.
  • Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) → Surgical Decompression
  • Bladder pressure monitoring guides intervention.
  • Emergent laparotomy if ACS confirmed.
Cardiogenic Shock:

Cardiogenic shock is caused by severe heart failure, leading to inadequate cardiac output and end-organ hypoperfusion. It can result from:

1. Myocardial Causes
  • Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) (most common)
  • Myocarditis
  • Cardiomyopathies (e.g., dilated, hypertrophic)
  • Ventricular aneurysm
  • Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

2. Mechanical Causes

  • Valvular disease (acute mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis)
  • Ventricular septal rupture
  • Papillary muscle rupture (post-MI)
  • Pericardial tamponade

3. Arrhythmic Causes

  • Bradyarrhythmias (severe sinus bradycardia, complete heart block)
  • Tachyarrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response)
Clinical Presentation
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg)
  • Cold, clammy extremities (poor perfusion)
  • Tachycardia (except in bradyarrhythmic causes)
  • Pulmonary congestion (if LV failure):
  • Dyspnea, crackles, pulmonary edema
  • JVD & peripheral edema (if RV failure)
  • Altered mental status, oliguria (low urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr)
Diagnosis
  • Hemodynamic Criteria for Cardiogenic Shock
  • SBP < 90 mmHg (for >30 min)
  • Cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m²
  • Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) > 18 mmHg
  • Elevated lactate > 2 mmol/L (tissue hypoxia)
Diagnostic Workup
  • ECG: ST-elevation MI (STEMI), arrhythmias
  • Echocardiography: Evaluates LV function, valve disease, tamponade
  • Pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz): Confirms low cardiac index & high PCWP
  • Cardiac enzymes (troponin, BNP): Detects myocardial injury or overload
  • Chest X-ray: Pulmonary congestion, enlarged heart
  • ABG/Lactate: Metabolic acidosis & tissue hypoperfusion
Management
A. Immediate Stabilization
1. Airway & Breathing
  • Oxygen, Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) if mild
  • Intubation & mechanical ventilation if severe pulmonary edema
  • Avoid excessive positive-pressure ventilation (reduces preload)

2. Circulatory Support

  • IV Fluids (cautiously!)
    • Small 250-500 mL boluses ONLY if hypovolemia
  • Vasopressors (if MAP < 65 mmHg)
    • First-line: Norepinephrine
    • Alternative: Dopamine (for bradycardia-related shock)
  • Inotropes (if CO is low)
    • Dobutamine (increases contractility)
    • Milrinone (for patients on beta-blockers)
  • Diuretics (if pulmonary edema)
    • Furosemide 20-40 mg IV (if volume overload)
B. Targeted Therapies Based on Cause
CauseTreatment
STEMI/NSTEMIUrgent PCI or CABG
Valvular DiseaseSurgery (valve repair/replacement)
Ventricular Septal RuptureEmergency surgery
TamponadePericardiocentesis
ArrhythmiasCardioversion (if unstable), antiarrhythmics
Severe LV DysfunctionMechanical circulatory support (IABP, ECMO)
C. Advanced Therapies
1. Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP)
  • Improves coronary perfusion and reduces afterload
  • Use in: Acute MI, severe LV failure

2. Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO)

  • Temporary biventricular support
  • Indications: Cardiogenic shock not responding to vasopressors/inotropes

3. Ventricular Assist Device (VADs)

  • Used as bridge to heart transplantation
  • Considered in end-stage heart failure
Neurogenic Shock:

Neurogenic shock occurs due to failure of the autonomic nervous system, leading to loss of vascular tone and severe hypotension. It results from:

1. Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
  • Above T6 → Sympathetic denervation → Profound hypotension & bradycardia
  • Below T6 → Hypotension with compensatory tachycardia

2. Anesthetic Causes

  • Spinal or epidural anesthesia (blocking sympathetic outflow)
  • General anesthesia with excessive vasodilation
3. Pharmacologic Causes
  • Autonomic blocking agents (e.g., alpha- or beta-blockers)

4. Trauma & Brain Injury

  • Brainstem trauma affecting sympathetic output
Clinical Features
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg, MAP < 65 mmHg)
  • Bradycardia (HR < 60 bpm) if lesion above T6
  • Warm, flushed skin below injury level (vasodilation)
  • Decreased cardiac output & stroke volume
  • Neurologic deficits (paralysis, sensory loss, areflexia in SCI)
Key Differentiation:
  • Spinal Cord Injury → Neurogenic Shock (Hypotension + Bradycardia)
  • Head Trauma → NOT Neurogenic Shock (Cushing’s Reflex: HTN + Bradycardia)

A. Immediate Stabilization
1. Airway & Breathing
  • If high cervical injury (C3-C5) → Intubate! (Diaphragmatic paralysis)
  • Spinal immobilization to prevent further injury
  • Oxygen therapy

2. Circulatory Support

  • IV Fluids (First-Line)
    • Start with 1-2 L of isotonic crystalloid (LR or NS)
    • Monitor MAP (goal > 85-90 mmHg for spinal cord perfusion)
  • Vasopressors (if fluids are insufficient)
    • Norepinephrine (First-line if bradycardia)
    • Phenylephrine (If HR is normal or high)
    • Dopamine (If bradycardia + hypotension)
B. Supportive & Definitive Therapy
1. Positioning
  • Trendelenburg position (if no contraindications) to improve venous return
  • Spinal immobilization (cervical collar, backboard)

2. Neuroprotection & ICU Monitoring

  • Monitor for secondary spinal cord injury
  • MAP goal: 85-90 mmHg for at least 7 days (to prevent spinal ischemia)
  • Foley catheter to monitor urine output

3. Atropine (For Severe Bradycardia)

  • 0.5 mg IV, repeat every 3-5 min (max: 3 mg total)
  • Consider transcutaneous pacing if refractory

4. DVT Prophylaxis (Due to prolonged immobility)

  • LMWH or Heparin

Low-output Inflammatory (Septic) shock:

Inflammatory shock (also known as septic shock) occurs due to systemic inflammation that leads to vascular dysfunction and hypoperfusion. It can result from:

  • Intra-abdominal sepsis (bowel perforation, ischemia, necrosis, abscesses,
  • peritonitis)
  • Soft tissue infections (necrotizing fasciitis, gangrene, infected burns)
  • Ischemia-reperfusion injury (massive trauma, inadequate resuscitation)
  • Inflammatory shock mimics hypovolemic shock due to massive plasma
  • leakage from microvascular endothelial disruption.
Clinical Features
  • Hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg, SBP < 90 mmHg)
  • Adrenergic discharge (tachycardia, vasoconstriction)
  • Oliguria (urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr)
  • Metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis due to poor perfusion)
  • Mental status changes (obtundation, confusion, lethargy)
  • ECG: ST-T wave changes (suggestive of ischemia due to hypoperfusion)
  • Fever (hyperthermia) or hypothermia (in severe cases)
Differentiation from Hypovolemic Shock:
  • Septic shock → Warm skin (early), later becomes cold & mottled
  • Hypovolemic shock → Cool, clammy skin from the start

Management
A. Immediate Resuscitation (Sepsis Bundle)
1. Fluids First (30 mL/kg Crystalloids)
  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) or Normal Saline (NS)
  • Goal: MAP > 65 mmHg, urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/hr
  • Monitor for fluid overload (lung exam, IVC ultrasound)

2. Early Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics (Within 1 Hour)

  • Community-acquired sepsis: Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime + Metronidazole
  • Hospital-acquired sepsis: Meropenem or Cefepime + Vancomycin
  • Necrotizing soft tissue infections: Vancomycin + Piperacillin- Tazobactam + Clindamycin

3. Vasopressors (If Fluids Fail)

  • First-line: Norepinephrine (maintains perfusion)
  • If persistent hypotension: Add Vasopressin or Epinephrine
  • MAP Goal: Maintain > 65 mmHg
B. Definitive Source Control
1. Surgery for Intra-Abdominal Sepsis
  • Laparotomy for bowel perforation, ischemia, abscess drainage
  • Necrotizing fasciitis: Early debridement, possible amputation

2. Drainage of Infected Fluid Collections

  • Percutaneous drainage for abscesses (CT or US-guided)

3. Debridement of Necrotic Tissue

  • Gangrene, ischemic limbs, infected wounds
C. Supportive ICU Care
1. Oxygenation & Mechanical Ventilation (If needed)
  • For ARDS or respiratory failure

2. Blood Sugar Control

  • Maintain glucose < 180 mg/dL with insulin infusion

3. DVT & Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis

  • Heparin/Enoxaparin (DVT prophylaxis)
  • Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for GI stress ulcer prevention
High-output Inflammatory (Septic) shock:

High-output inflammatory shock is an early phase of septic shock, characterized by increased cardiac output with systemic vasodilation. It may precede low- output shock or occur after successful resuscitation of low-output shock.

Key Characteristics
  • Hypotension despite high cardiac output
  • Warm, well-perfused extremities (vasodilation)
  • Fever (not always present)
  • High oxygen consumption (1.5x normal)
  • Bounding pulses
  • Wide pulse pressure (SBP − DBP is elevated)
  • Metabolic acidosis due to poor perfusion
Progression to Low-Output Shock

If untreated, progressive vasodilation and capillary leak lead to low cardiac output, cold extremities, and organ failure.

  • Lactated Ringer’s (LR) or Normal Saline (NS), 30 mL/kg IV bolus

2. Optimize Cardiac Function

  • Check ventricular end-diastolic volume (via CVP or echocardiography)
  • If adequate preload → Use inotropes (Dobutamine)
  • If inadequate preload → Give more fluids

  • Risk of limb, gut, kidney ischemia
  • Only use vasopressors (Norepinephrine) if fluids & inotropes fail

  • Necrotizing soft tissue infections: Vancomycin + Piperacillin- Tazobactam + Clindamycin

  • Debridement for infected wounds, gangrene

Common physiological responses to shock:
I. Neurohumoral Responses

Shock triggers neurohumoral compensatory mechanisms to maintain circulatory homeostasis and perfusion to vital organs.

1️- Sympathetic Adrenergic Response
  • Vasoconstriction: Arterioles, venules, and small veins (except heart & brain) constrict → ↑ BP & perfusion to heart & brain
  • ↑ Myocardial contractility → Augments cardiac output
  • ↑ Heart rate (tachycardia) → To maintain cardiac output
2️- Hormonal Responses
HormoneFunction in Shock
Angiotensin IIVasoconstriction (skin, kidneys, splanchnic organs) → ↑ BP
& shunts blood to heart & brain. Stimulates aldosterone
release for sodium retention.
Vasopressin (ADH)Constricts peripheral vessels, retains water, and increases blood pressure without reducing kidney perfusion.
CortisolIncreases glucose, reduces inflammation, and enhances
vascular response to catecholamines.
Glucagon & EpinephrineIncreases blood glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
II. Metabolic Responses
  • Intracellular acidosis → H⁺ exchanged for Na⁺ & Cl⁻ → Cell swelling (~3L intracellular volume gain)
  • Hyperglycemia due to stress hormones → Prevents hypoglycemia, but excess glucose can worsen osmotic diuresis → Avoid glucose-containing fluids in resuscitation
  • Increased plasma oncotic pressure → Draws interstitial fluid back into circulation
III. Microvascular Responses

In severe shock, three pathologic microvascular responses worsen the patient's condition:

1️- Arteriolar Vasodilation & Capillary Leak
  • Loss of vascular tone → Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
  • Plasma extravasation → Fluid shifts into interstitial space → Edema
  • Massive third-spacing in septic shock → Pulmonary, cerebral, or peripheral edema
2️- Endothelial Disruption
  • Inflammatory mediators (cytokines, leukotrienes, thromboxanes, fibrin degradation products, ROS) damage the endothelium.
  • Microvascular thrombosis impairs capillary perfusion, contributing to organ failure.
3️- Microvascular Embolization
  • White cell & platelet aggregates lodge in lungs & liver
  • Triggers further vasodilation & inflammation, worsening capillary leak
IV. Ultrasound in Shock Diagnosis & Resuscitation

Modern noninvasive bedside ultrasound (US) has replaced many invasive monitoring methods (CVP, Swan-Ganz catheters) for shock assessment.
